A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same representation-similarity and aligned-training work, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original DeiT, BERT and GPT-2 experiments, alongside MNIST residual-connection tests and transferability evaluations.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds saturation analyses, loss-weight ablations, neural-collapse measurements, DETR results and CLIP analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix B.5 extends intermediate-layer supervision to DETR's decoder through auxiliary decoding losses for object-class and bounding-box predictions. The central shared-classifier objective, linearly increasing layer weights and alternating training remain unchanged. V2's explicit odd/even iteration schedule clarifies an approach already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: V2 adds object detection with DETR and multimodal representation analysis using CLIP on CIFAR-10 images paired with label prompts. These introduce different task requirements and input modalities. Existing classification, language-generation, MNIST and transfer evaluations remain; RTE and QQP results are relocated, not removed. The detection dataset is not identified.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 15 adds a uniform-weight aligned-training variant as a comparator to linearly increasing weights. The existing standard-training, multi-exit/classifiers and cosine-regularization comparisons remain. CKA regularization is newly discussed but is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include saturation-layer counting, DETR AP50, CLIP within- and cross-modality comparisons, and controlled LLaMA decoding examples. The depth comparison changes from validation accuracy in v1 Figure 4(a) to training accuracy in v2 Figure 5(a). GPT-2's printed accuracy normalization changes from 1/(nD) to 1/D in Equation 20; the PDFs do not establish that its scores were recomputed.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of saturation versus similarity, uniform versus increasing loss weights, layerwise neural collapse, LLaMA prediction stability and CLIP alignment. Existing residual-connection and transferability tests are largely retained. V1's PCA trajectories and residual-angle analysis disappear.

E5.justification: Both versions report sample-wise distributions through box plots, including cosine similarities and residual norm ratios. Neither reports repeated-seed performance estimates, run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2 does not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds saturation results, the shallow-versus-final-layer weighting tradeoff, neural-collapse curves, DETR AP50, CLIP similarities and parameter-count comparisons in Table 1. Its depth plot reports training rather than validation results. The principal ImageNet early-exit results remain unchanged: aligned training achieves 77.96% at 1.36× speedup, versus 78.32% at 1.42× for multiple classifiers.

T1.justification: V1 has no corresponding theorems or proofs. V2 introduces a Wasserstein-geodesic assumption, theorems asserting monotonic representation similarity and predicted probability, and proofs in Appendix A. It also formalizes saturation layers and epsilon-effective depth.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion now claim theoretical justification for representation progression and saturation, including that increasing predicted probability preserves correct predictions across subsequent layers. Earlier saturation becomes an explicit claimed benefit of aligned training. The original single-classifier and comparable multi-exit performance claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting similarity to saturation and effective-depth generalization, explains the loss-weight tradeoff and insufficient discriminative guidance from cosine regularization, and discusses CLIP's modality gap. It explicitly qualifies the geodesic assumption as approximate. V1's residual-orthogonality and internal-covariate-shift explanations are removed.

D1.justification: V2 specifies odd/even loss alternation, LLaMA decoding details, and CLIP token extraction, projections and text prompts. Most original training hyperparameters and GPT-2's training budget remain unchanged. Hardware reporting becomes inconsistent: Appendix B states four GPUs for NLP, while Appendix C.2 retains the single-GPU description.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly connects intermediate predictions to logit lens and Geva et al.'s saturation work, and develops substantial connections to geodesic dynamics and effective-depth literature. DETR, CLIP and modality-gap research also enter the discussion. This broadens the scientific positioning beyond citation-format changes.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, its abstract and contribution narrative are substantially revised, and Sections 2–3 gain a new organization. Language applications become Section 3.2, transferability details move to Appendix B.4, and the appendices are reorganized around proofs, vision, language and multimodal studies.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces PCA panels with reorganized similarity/accuracy comparisons and cumulative saturation. V2 adds a parameter table and numerous saturation, ablation, neural-collapse, detection, LLaMA and CLIP displays. Transferability plots move to the appendix, and the six-panel GLUE display is split between main text and appendix.

improvement.justification: The new weighting ablation, neural-collapse measurements and broader applications provide useful support absent from v1. However, the new theoretical centerpiece has a substantive gap: Appendix A.2 assumes equal intermediate feature norms and a restricted update direction absent from Theorem 2's statement. Equation 20 also drops the existing accuracy metric's token-count normalization. These empirical gains and new correctness problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
